title: Cleaning, Disinfection, and Sterile vs Clean Technique

unit.title: Clinical Office Practice and Patient Safety

sections.learningObjectives:
- Distinguish cleaning, disinfection, and sterilization, including what each process does and does not accomplish.
- Distinguish sterile (surgical) technique from clean (medical) technique and identify the tasks for which each is appropriate.
- Apply the correct level of processing (cleaning, low-level or high-level disinfection, or sterilization) to a given item or task using the Spaulding classification.
- Recognize safety and escalation responsibilities in reprocessing, environmental cleaning, and aseptic practice, including bloodborne-pathogen and chemical safety.
sections.eli10:
### Question 1

Cleaning is like washing a muddy plate with soapy water and scrubbing it. It takes the dirt off, but it does not promise to kill every single germ.

### Question 2

Disinfection is like using a special cleaning spray on a counter that kills most of the bad germs, though it might miss the very toughest ones.

### Question 3

Sterilization is like baking something in an oven so hot that nothing at all, not even the toughest little seeds, can survive.

### Question 4

You always wash a plate before you put it in the sanitizer, so the sanitizer can actually reach the surface.

### Question 5

Wiping a table with soapy water makes it look clean, but it does not get rid of the hidden germs that you cannot see.

### Question 6

An antiseptic is like the gentle, safe soap you put on a cut, while a disinfectant is the stronger stuff you use on counters and floors.

### Question 7

The places lots of people touch all day, like a door handle, are the places that need the most wiping, because that is where germs get passed around.

### Question 8

It is like sorting your laundry by how dirty it is: the things that touch the most delicate, important spots get the most careful cleaning.

### Question 9

Items that only touch unbroken skin, like a blood pressure cuff, just need a good clean and a light germ-killing wipe, not the heavy-duty treatment.

### Question 10

Tools that go inside the body in a place that must stay germ-free have to be made completely germ-free first.

### Question 11

Tools that touch the soft, wet inside parts of the body need an extra-strong germ-killing wash, stronger than what a countertop needs.

### Question 12

A blood pressure cuff only touches skin that is not broken, so a good clean and a light germ-kill is plenty.

### Question 13

The germ-killing spray is like a timer on a washing machine: it has to run for the full time to do its job properly.

### Question 14

You should use the special germ-killer that is made for doctor offices and follow the directions on the bottle, not just any spray that smells nice.

### Question 15

When blood spills, you put on your safety gear, clean up the mess, and then kill the germs, following the office rules step by step.

### Question 16

Germs can hide under the blood like bugs hiding under a leaf, so you have to wipe the blood away first for the germ-killer to reach them.

### Question 17

When you clean up something yucky, you wear your safety gloves and anything else the rules say, so the bad stuff does not get on your skin.

### Question 18

Scrubbing is what actually lifts the dirt off, like rubbing a crayon mark until it comes off instead of just looking at it.

### Question 19

If your cleaning rag gets really dirty, you swap it for a fresh one, because a dirty rag just moves the mess around instead of cleaning it.

### Question 20

Even if a table looks fine, you still wipe it down with germ-killer between people, because germs can hide where you cannot see them.

### Question 21

The strong cleaner for counters is too harsh for your skin, just like you would not use heavy-duty floor cleaner as hand soap.

### Question 22

Bacterial spores are like tough little seeds that survive almost everything, so sterilizing equipment means making sure even those seeds are destroyed.

### Question 23

An autoclave is like a super-hot pressure cooker that uses very hot steam to kill every germ on the tools.

### Question 24

Pressure lets the steam get even hotter than normal boiling water, and that extra heat is what wipes out the toughest germs.

### Question 25

The best proof the machine worked is putting in a tiny test packet of super-tough germs and checking that they all died.

### Question 26

The color-changing tape is like a receipt that says the oven was on, but it does not tell you for sure that every germ was cooked.

### Question 27

Before the tools go in the hot steamer, you wash them, dry them, and wrap them in special paper the steam can pass through.

### Question 28

If you stuff too many tools into the steamer, the hot steam cannot get around every one, like trying to rinse a whole sink full of dishes at once.

### Question 29

If the wrapped tools come out wet, they are not safe to use anymore, so they go back through the steamer, just like soggy packaging is not clean packaging.

### Question 30

A wrapped tool stays germ-free as long as its wrapper is not torn or wet and it is stored in a clean, dry place.

### Question 31

If the wrapper has a rip in it, the tools inside are no longer germ-free, so they get re-cleaned instead of used on a patient.

### Question 32

You should never use a mystery liquid from a bottle with no label, because you cannot be sure what it is or if it is safe.

### Question 33

Sterile packages live in a clean, dry cupboard, not under a drippy sink or on the floor, so they stay clean and dry.

### Question 34

Clean technique is like keeping things tidy and washing your hands so germs stay low in number, not making everything perfectly germ-free.

### Question 35

Sterile technique is the very strict way of keeping everything completely germ-free, used when the body is opened or something is put inside.

### Question 36

If something is going inside the body or through the skin, you use the super-strict germ-free rules to keep infection out.

### Question 37

Simple things like checking blood pressure on unbroken skin just need clean, careful handling, not the full germ-free setup.

### Question 38

Sterile gloves are for the extra-careful germ-free jobs, while ordinary clean gloves are fine for everyday cleaning and touching.

### Question 39

A sterile field is like a protected clean zone on a table where only germ-free things are allowed to touch, like a no-shoes zone.

### Question 40

Imagine the outside edge of the clean cloth is a no-touch border, like the line around a swimming pool you stay away from.

### Question 41

Keep germ-free things up high where you can see them; anything that dips down low is treated as no longer clean.

### Question 42

When the cloth gets wet, germs can soak right through it, like a puddle leaking through paper, so it is no longer safe.

### Question 43

You keep your eyes on the clean zone the whole time, like watching a pot so it does not boil over, because a mistake you miss can ruin it.

### Question 44

Reaching over the clean zone is like shaking a dusty sleeve over a plate of food; little bits can drop down and mess it up.

### Question 45

If something clean gets dirtied by mistake, you speak up and swap it for a fresh one instead of quietly using the dirty one.

### Question 46

You only grab the inside cuff with your bare fingers, and once one glove is on, that clean glove touches only the clean part of the next glove.

### Question 47

Once the clean gloves are on, they can only touch other clean things, never your face or the table.

### Question 48

Washing your hands is the single best way to keep germs from moving from one person to another.

### Question 49

Clean gloves are like a barrier that keeps the germs on your hands from getting onto the patient, but they are not the same as sterile gloves.

### Question 50

You throw away the gloves after each person and wash your hands, then put on a brand-new pair for the next person.

### Question 51

If something clean falls on the floor, you get a fresh one, because the floor is full of germs no matter how it looks.

### Question 52

You peel the wrapper open carefully, without reaching over or blowing on the clean stuff inside, so it stays germ-free.

### Question 53

You pour a little into the sink first to rinse the bottle's edge, then carefully pour into the clean bowl without letting the bottle touch anything.

### Question 54

You set up the clean zone right before you need it and keep watching it, like preparing a plate of food just before serving.

### Question 55

When you are not sure how to clean a tool, you check the instruction sheet and the office rule book instead of guessing.

### Question 56

If the germ-killer looks cloudy and is past its date, you throw it out and get a fresh bottle instead of using the old one.

### Question 57

Some cleaning liquids can turn into a dangerous gas if you mix them, so you never pour two different ones together.

### Question 58

Some tools are like paper cups: made to be used once and then thrown away, not washed and used again.

### Question 59

Used needles go straight into a special hard box so no one gets poked, and you never try to put the cap back on with your hands.

### Question 60

If a needle really has to be capped, you use a safe trick with one hand so your fingers are never near the point.

### Question 61

If the test germs survive, the machine did not work, so you stop using it, keep those tools aside, and call for it to be fixed and re-tested.

### Question 62

Give the tools some space in the steamer so the hot steam can swirl around every one of them.

### Question 63

Before a careful procedure, the skin gets wiped with a safe germ-reducing liquid made for skin, not the strong cleaner for counters.

### Question 64

When you are not sure if something stayed clean, you treat it as dirty and get a fresh one, just to be safe.

### Question 65

The extra-strong germ-killer wipes out almost everything but a few tough spores; sterilizing wipes out absolutely everything, even those.

### Question 66

Clean the things people actually touch and use first, like the exam table and the equipment, not the dusty high shelves.

### Question 67

Wash your hands before you put gloves on and wash them again after you take the gloves off.

### Question 68

Wear gloves and gently put the dirty sheets into a special bag, without shaking them, so the germs do not fly around.

### Question 69

Think of three steps: wipe the dirt off, kill most germs, then kill every germ including the toughest ones.

### Question 70

If blood touches a cut on your skin, you stop right away, wash it with soap and water, and tell a supervisor so you can get help.

### Question 71

The rule is: if the procedure goes inside the body or through the skin, use the strict germ-free method; the office rules and the clinician confirm it.

### Question 72

The part of the clean cloth that hangs down under the table edge is like the floor; you do not touch it or put things on it.

### Question 73

Keep the surface wet with the germ-killer for the whole three minutes, like letting a cleaner soak in before you wipe it away.

### Question 74

When you are not sure, ask the person in charge and follow the office rules instead of making up your own answer.

### Question 75

The safety instructions for a cleaner live on its label and in a special fact sheet, just like a fire extinguisher has instructions on it.

### Question 76

Wipe the clean spots first and the dirty spots last, and go from the top down, so the mess does not get dragged onto clean places.

### Question 77

Your job is to keep the office surfaces clean and germ-safe by following the office rules, and to speak up if something is broken or missing.

### Question 78

Only germ-free things can go on the germ-free zone, because one dirty thing makes the whole zone dirty.

### Question 79

Clean things can only touch other clean things; if a clean thing touches a dirty thing, it is no longer clean.

### Question 80

Keep the germ-free tools on their own labeled shelf, separate from the regular clean stuff, so no one grabs the wrong one.

### Question 81

Before opening, give the wrapper a careful check for rips, damp spots, and the right label, so you know it is safe.

### Question 82

Putting the date and batch number on the package is like a receipt, so if something goes wrong you know exactly which tools to check.

### Question 83

You dry the tools before wrapping them, because wrapping wet things makes the package come out damp and not safe.

### Question 84

Before using a new cleaner, read the directions on the bottle so you know how much to use, how long to wait, and what to wear.

### Question 85

The instruction sheet tells you exactly how to clean a tool so it stays safe to use on people, and you follow it every time.
